title: Paano Magtanim ng Luyang Dilaw: How to Plant Turmeric the Traditional Way
metaTitle: Paano Magtanim ng Luyang Dilaw: The Traditional Way
metaDescription: Paano magtanim ng luyang dilaw? See how traditional farmers plant luyang dilaw step by step, with the days and what to change for a higher yield.
excerpt: Paano magtanim ng luyang dilaw? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant luyang dilaw (turmeric), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: A farm worker planting in a field

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant luyang dilaw. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino growers usually raise luyang dilaw from rhizome pieces on beds or ridges, often in backyards and under coconut, and dig it seven to ten months later for cooking, salabat and powder. For small growers who want the usual way and what to change for a bigger, brighter harvest.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for root crops](/land-preparation/root-crop-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [luyang dilaw nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/turmeric-nutrient-deficiency).
When to plant luyang dilaw
Planted like ginger as the rains begin, around April to June, so the shoots grow on the rains. The leaves dry down in the cool dry months, when the rhizomes are dug.
What you plant

Whole or split mother rhizomes and finger rhizomes from a healthy clump, kept from the last harvest. Pick firm, plump, disease free pieces with buds. A full hectare needs a lot of seed, around 2,500 kg, which is why most growers start small and multiply their own.
Paano magtanim ng luyang dilaw, step by step
The crop is ready about 270 days after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 14 days before planting: Plow until fine
items.text: With the first rains, plow and harrow several times until the soil is loose and fine. Lime very sour soils.

items.title: 3 days before planting: Make beds or ridges
items.text: Form beds about 1 m wide and 15 cm high with 50 cm paths, or ridges and furrows 45 to 60 cm apart. Pick land that never floods.

blocks.text: The nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 1 day before planting: Ready the seed pieces
items.text: Split the clumps into mother and finger pieces with buds, and set aside any that are soft, shriveled or discolored.

parts.title: Keep seed clumps in the shade
parts.text: Set aside healthy clumps at harvest and keep them in a shaded, airy place under a cover of leaves until the first rains. Throw out any that turn soft, shriveled or discolored while they wait.

parts.title: Split mothers from fingers
parts.text: Break each clump into the round mother rhizome and the long finger rhizomes. Big mothers can be split in two. Both kinds grow, as long as each piece is plump and carries buds.

parts.title: Dip them if rot was a problem
parts.text: Where soft rot or scale insects showed last season, some growers dip the seed pieces in a fungicide or insecticide before storing them and again before planting, following the label. Badly hit pieces are thrown out, not stored.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant in small pits with manure
items.text: Dig small holes about 25 by 30 cm apart on the beds, or 25 cm apart along the ridges. Put rotted manure or compost in each hole, set a seed piece on it and cover with soil.

items.title: Day 1: Mulch with green leaves
items.text: Cover the beds with cut leaves or grass right after planting to keep the soil moist and stop weeds.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 45: Weed, fertilize and earth up
items.text: Pull the weeds, put the first fertilizer along the rows, pull soil up around the shoots and add fresh mulch.

items.title: Day 60: Watch for shoot borer and rot
items.text: Look for holes with frass on the stems and a dead center shoot, brown leaf blotches, and soft, collapsing stems at the base. Pull and burn rotting plants.

items.title: Day 90: Second weeding and earthing up
items.text: Weed again, give the rest of the fertilizer, earth up and renew the mulch.

items.title: Day 120: Last weeding
items.text: Weed once more if needed. After this the leaves shade the beds.

items.title: Day 271: Clean, keep seed and dry the rest
items.text: Soak off the soil and trim the roots. Keep healthy clumps in the shade for the next planting. For powder, many boil the rhizomes, then sun dry them for about a week before grinding.

parts.title: Soak off the soil
parts.text: Put the clumps in water to loosen the soil, then rinse them and pull off the long roots and the dry leaf scales.

parts.title: Keep the seed apart
parts.text: Choose the healthiest clumps for the next planting before anything else and store them in the shade. Only the rest goes on to be boiled and dried.

parts.title: Boil until soft
parts.text: Boil the cleaned rhizomes in a big pot of water until a sharp stick pushes in easily. Boiled turmeric dries faster and keeps a more even color.

parts.title: Sun dry for about a week
parts.text: Spread the boiled rhizomes thinly on mats or a clean floor in full sun and turn them often. Pile and cover them at night and when rain comes, until they are hard and snap cleanly.

parts.title: Store dry, grind as needed
parts.text: Keep the dry pieces in sealed bags or jars in a dry place, and grind only what you will sell or use soon so the powder keeps its color and smell.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 270: Dig when the leaves dry
items.text: Turmeric is ready when the leaves and stems dry up, about 7 to 10 months after planting. Cut the dry leaves, loosen the soil and lift the clumps by hand without breaking them.

blocks.text: Watering luyang dilaw, stage by stage

Luyang dilaw is rain fed on most farms, planted with the first rains around April to June on beds or ridges and mulched with green leaves. In long dry spells growers water by furrow or hose, and the leaves dry down in the cool dry months when the rhizomes are dug. Mostly rain. In dry spells growers water by furrow between the ridges or by hose. Water in the morning.

blocks.title: Never let luyang dilaw go dry at these stages
blocks.text: The weeks after planting, until the shoots are up. Leaf growth, when the plant needs steady moisture.

blocks.caption: Watering schedule for luyang dilaw, stage by stage
rows: Plant into moist soil with the first rains and mulch at once. Water in a dry week
Moisten the soil under the mulch, no standing water
Rain is usually enough. In dry spells water by furrow or hose, more often on sandy soil than on clay
A soaking that wets the bed, then drain
Keep the soil moist in dry spells. Water less as the rains end
Stop watering as the leaves and stems dry

blocks.text:
**Without irrigation.** Plant with the first rains so the leaves grow through the wet months, on beds or ridges in land that never floods. Cover the beds with cut leaves or grass right after planting to hold moisture and stop weeds.

**In the dry season.** An irrigated crop gets about 15 to 23 waterings in the whole season on clay soil and about 40 on sandy loam, given in the dry spells while the leaves grow. Water when the soil under the mulch is dry or the leaves roll in the morning.

**In the rainy season.** Use raised beds or ridges and pick land that never floods: turmeric cannot stand waterlogging. In soaked soil the stem base turns soft and the plant collapses as the rhizomes rot.

items: **Too little water:** Leaves roll and brown at the edges, growth stalls and the rhizomes stay small.
**Too much water:** Leaves yellow, the stem base goes soft and water soaked, and the plants collapse as the rhizomes rot.

blocks.text: To water better for a higher yield: A thick mulch of green leaves or straw holds moisture and cuts the number of waterings. Where water is at hand, watering through dry spells in the leaf growth months gives bigger rhizomes.
Spacing, water and fertilizer for luyang dilaw
Spacing
Beds about 1 m wide with plants about 25 by 30 cm apart, or ridges 45 to 60 cm apart with plants about 25 cm apart. One seed piece a hole.
Water

Rainfed in most farms, planted with the first rains. It needs steady moisture while leaves grow but cannot stand waterlogging, so beds or ridges are used. In long dry spells growers water by furrow or hose.
Fertilizer

Most backyard growers use only rotted manure or compost in the planting holes and as mulch. Larger plantings add complete fertilizer and potash in two or three splits during the weedings, since turmeric, like ginger, needs a lot of potash. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-plants).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Mulching after planting, weeding at about 45 to 60, 90 and 120 days, earthing up and fresh mulch with each fertilizer, and light shade at most. It is often grown between coconut trees or with corn or chili.
When and how to harvest

Dug about 7 to 10 months after planting, when the leaves and stems dry. Clumps are lifted carefully, cleaned by soaking, and the best ones kept for seed. The rest are sold fresh or boiled, sun dried and ground into powder.
Common mistakes when planting luyang dilaw

items: Planting soft or shriveled seed pieces, which spreads rhizome rot.
Planting in low spots that flood in heavy rain.
Leaving the beds bare, so weeds take over and the soil dries.
Too much shade under dense trees, which cuts the yield.
Digging before the leaves dry, so the rhizomes are watery and pale.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of luyang dilaw
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Use healthy, firm seed rhizomes from clean clumps, and multiply your own stock before expanding.
Test the soil and fertilize by the result, with enough potash and plenty of compost.
Plant on raised beds or ridges and mulch after every weeding.
Grow it in light shade only and rotate with crops outside the ginger family.
Dry and grind in clean conditions if you sell powder, so the color and smell stay strong.

items.q: When do farmers plant luyang dilaw in the Philippines?
items.a: Planted like ginger as the rains begin, around April to June, so the shoots grow on the rains. The leaves dry down in the cool dry months, when the rhizomes are dug.

items.q: How far apart do you plant luyang dilaw?
items.a: Beds about 1 m wide with plants about 25 by 30 cm apart, or ridges 45 to 60 cm apart with plants about 25 cm apart. One seed piece a hole.

items.q: How long before luyang dilaw can be harvested?
items.a: It is ready about 270 days after planting. Dug about 7 to 10 months after planting, when the leaves and stems dry.

items.q: How often do you water luyang dilaw?
items.a: Planting and shoots coming up, planting day to day 45: Plant into moist soil with the first rains and mulch at once. Water in a dry week. Leaf growth, day 45 to 150: Rain is usually enough. In dry spells water by furrow or hose, more often on sandy soil than on clay. Rhizomes filling, day 150 to 240: Keep the soil moist in dry spells. Water less as the rains end. An irrigated crop gets about 15 to 23 waterings in the whole season on clay soil and about 40 on sandy loam, given in the dry spells while the leaves grow.

items.q: What do you plant to grow luyang dilaw?
items.a: Whole or split mother rhizomes and finger rhizomes from a healthy clump, kept from the last harvest. Pick firm, plump, disease free pieces with buds.
